Correspondence: tianyd@amazon.com . Tianyu Ding Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Email: tianyd@amazon.com Jianhong Xin Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Email: xijianho@amazon.com Juan Pablo De la Cruz Weinstein Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Email: jcruam@amazon.com Abstract Long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning can learn from outcome verification, but its trajectory-level advantage is broadcast across many reasoning, API, and answer tokens. Self-distillation promises a denser signal by reusing a policy’s own rollouts or a privileged teacher. We show, however, that direct token-level self-distillation can silently destroy tool use: it rehearses teacher behavior without knowing which actions the verifier rewards, so useful skills and harmful shortcuts are amplified together. We introduce Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation (SGCD) , which uses distillation for credit assignment rather than as a competing actor loss. Dynamic sampling produces mixed successful and failed sibling rollouts; an external LLM summarizes their contrast into a training-only stepwise credit reference; dense teacher/student divergence drives credit reassignment; and bounded detached credit weights reshape GRPO token advantages. The deployed student sees no external LLM, sibling evidence, or oracle. Across AppWorld and τ 3 \tau^{3} -airline, SGCD improves over matched GRPO comparators: AppWorld TGC 42.9 → 45.6 42.9\to 45.6 on test_normal and 24.7 → 27.0 24.7\to 27.0 on test_challenge , and τ 3 \tau^{3} -airline pass@1 0.583 → 0.602 0.583\to 0.602 . 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning for multi-turn, tool-using agents increasingly relies on group-relative policy-gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . These methods can learn from outcome verification alone, but their token-level credit assignment is coarse: the same trajectory-level advantage is broadcast across long sequences of reasoning, API calls, tool observations, and final answers. Self-distillation (SD) offers an attractive complement: use the policy’s own successful behavior, or a teacher conditioned on privileged training-time information, to supply a denser signal ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . The hard part is making that signal help the policy gradient rather than fight it. The hidden failure. We first show, on the τ 3 \tau^{3} -airline customer-service benchmark ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Barres et al., 2025 ; Sierra Research, 2026 ) , that naive SD actively degrades long-horizon tool-use. Over training, the model increasingly solves easy information-only cases without using tools, while state-changing action tasks collapse to zero success (§ 3 ). The aggregate score conceals the mechanism: the policy is not learning a better agent; it is abandoning executable tool-use behavior the base or supervised checkpoint already possessed. The lesson: use distillation for credit, not as a competing loss. The contrast with a GRPO+KL recipe is sharp: it preserves tool-use and reaches 0.583 0.583 test-split pass@1, whereas SDPO peaks at 0.317 0.317 and collapses on state-changing action tasks. Our subsequent AppWorld probes led to the same design constraint. Direct SD pressure can be live and non-inert, yet still degrade action quality when the teacher target is misaligned with what the verifier rewards; our strongest controlled ablation uses direct/uncapped SD and falls below the matched GRPO control. We therefore repurpose teacher/student divergence as a credit-assignment signal : it determines where the policy-gradient advantage should be concentrated, while the policy-gradient objective remains the model’s update driver. The method. We introduce Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation (SGCD) . Dynamic sampling produces mixed groups of sibling rollouts for the same task, giving verified successful and failed attempts under the same prompt. A strong external LLM summarizes those siblings into a stepwise credit reference: what the successful attempts checked, which branches failed, and where the failed attempts deviated. The current policy is then scored twice on the rollout: once under the ordinary student context and once under the credit reference as a stop-gradient teacher. Dense top- K K reverse-KL and entropy produce divergence-driven credit features; a bounded credit-weighting rule converts those features into clipped token-level advantage weights inside the GRPO surrogate (§ 4 ). No direct distillation loss is needed for the actor weights: distillation guides credit, and policy gradient performs the update. Why it is deployable. The external LLM, sibling evidence, and credit reference are training-only. The deployed student receives the same clean prompt as the GRPO policy: no oracle, no sibling rollouts, no external LLM, and no task-specific credit reference. Because the divergence signal is detached from the actor parameters and only reshapes the verified policy-gradient advantage, the method avoids the failure mode in which a privileged teacher distribution pulls the model toward actions that the clean deployment prompt cannot reproduce. Contributions. 1. A tool-use diagnosis: naive self-distillation can reinforce benchmark shortcuts, preserving easy information-only behavior while destroying state-changing action capability (§ 3 ). 2. SGCD : a sibling-guided credit-distillation method that builds a stepwise credit reference from mixed successful/failed rollouts and uses dense teacher/student divergence to reweight, not replace, the PG update (§ 4 ). 3. An empirical study on AppWorld and τ 3 \tau^{3} -airline. SGCD improves over a matched GRPO comparator on both benchmarks, and ablations show that sibling credit references, divergence-driven credit reassignment, and PG dominance are necessary for the gain (§ 5 ). 2 Background and Related Work Group-relative RL for tool-use agents. Policy-gradient reinforcement learning traces back to score-function estimators and the policy-gradient theorem ( Williams, 1992 ; Sutton et al., 1999 ) . PPO-style clipped policy optimization ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) remains the practical base for many RL fine-tuning recipes. GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) estimates advantages from groups of sampled rollouts without a learned value function; DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) adds Clip-Higher and dynamic sampling, keeping only mixed-outcome groups. We use GRPO as the policy-gradient backbone, borrowing the mixed-outcome sampling principle as an evidence source. Group-relative methods have become a practical backbone for reasoning and tool-use RL ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025 ) . SGCD keeps this policy-gradient backbone intact: its contribution is to reshape token credit inside the surrogate using sibling-derived evidence, not to replace the reward or train a separate value model. Knowledge distillation and privileged information. Classical knowledge distillation transfers information from teacher probabilities or features to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) ; learning under privileged information conditions a teacher or training signal on information unavailable at inference ( Vapnik and Izmailov, 2015 ) . Recent on-policy distillation work emphasizes that the student’s own samples reduce exposure mismatch ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . SGCD adopts this on-policy setting, but changes the role of the distributional comparison: dense teacher/student divergence becomes a detached credit signal for policy-gradient weighting rather than an actor-gradient KL objective. Self-distillation for RL. A family of recent methods adds self-distillation to group-relative RL. SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) replaces the reward with a teacher/student log-ratio advantage and uses successful peer rollouts as context. OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) adds a generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD; Lin, 1991 ) auxiliary to GRPO with a label-privileged teacher. Skill-SD ( Wang et al., 2026 ) distills from self-generated natural-language skill summaries with importance-weighted reverse-KL. SDAR ( Lu et al., 2026 ) gates token-level SD by an asymmetric σ ⁡ ( β ​ Δ ) \sigma(\beta\Delta) policy-shift gap; RLSD ( Chen et al., 2026 ) reports a related SD-RL ladder. These methods motivate teacher-side skills, sibling context, dense logit comparisons, and gates. Our negative result shows why, in long-horizon tool-use, the safe use is narrower: the distributional signal should identify where credit should move, while the verified policy gradient remains the only actor update driver. Self-distillation instability. Prior work reports that unconstrained self-distillation can collapse or drift when the teacher is noisy, overconfident, or instance-specific ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . We contribute a concrete tool-use instance: zero-tool collapse on τ 3 \tau^{3} -airline (§ 3 ). This failure is especially relevant to agents because a teacher can be confident about a locally plausible action sequence that is unreproducible under the clean deployment prompt. Positioning. SGCD differs from the closest SD-RL methods along three axes, with a compact comparison in Appendix Table 7 . First, it builds the privileged signal from mixed siblings : verified successful and failed rollouts for the same task, selected by dynamic sampling. Second, an external LLM converts those siblings into a stepwise credit reference, avoiding a persistent skill bank or inference-time dependency. Third, dense reverse-KL and entropy are used for divergence-driven credit reassignment and bounded advantage weights, rather than a standalone SD auxiliary. Thus the method is still distillation–the teacher comparison supplies knowledge–but the gradient path remains policy-gradient dominant by construction. We use “distillation” in this credit-transfer sense: teacher-side information is transferred through detached credit weights in the policy-gradient surrogate, not through a teacher-matching actor loss. 3 The Failure Mode: Naive SD Destroys Tool-Use Setup. We train Qwen3.5-4B on the τ 3 \tau^{3} -airline domain ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Barres et al., 2025 ; Sierra Research, 2026 ) and evaluate on a held-out 20-task split under greedy pass@1. Tasks are categorized by their gold action set into state-changing action tasks (booking/cancellation/update; 13 tasks), information-only tasks (4), transfer-only (1), and no-action (2). Aggregate result. Table 2 reports pass@1 across recipes. GRPO+KL reaches 0.583 0.583 ; SDPO peaks at 0.317 0.317 and scores 0 % 0\% on state-changing action tasks at late steps. The aggregate hides the mechanism. Mechanism: zero-tool collapse. A per-step rollout audit shows that SDPO shifts toward no-tool information-only successes: the no-tool share rises from 0 % 0\% to 100 % 100\% , while mean tools per success falls 2.5 → 0.0 2.5\to 0.0 . The GRPO+KL control stays at 0 % 0\% zero-tool. Thus SDPO is not merely trading off categories; it preserves easy information-only answers while abandoning executable action behavior, as Table 2 shows. Why direct SD fails. Stop-gradient on the teacher prevents updates to the teacher’s parameters, but the target distribution still defines where the student is pulled. When the teacher places probability mass on “skip the tool, answer directly” or on an action plan that is not supported by the clean deployment prompt, a KL/JSD auxiliary can faithfully optimize the wrong target.
